title: Explicitly map rubric scoring criteria to analysis outputs
when_to_use: When the task or rubric explicitly defines required metrics and analysis dimensions for scoring.
experience:
- Before writing any code, parse the task instructions and identify all rubric categories (e.g., Speed Metrics, Sequence Analysis).
- For each rubric criterion, write down the exact metric definition and expected output format.
- Map each required metric to the corresponding data source columns and aggregation logic.
- After analysis, verify your outputs match the rubric's specified anchor points (e.g., sample counts, baseline values).
- If data doesn't support a rubric requirement, document the gap and propose an alternative method aligned with the rubric's intent.
common_failure_prevented: Missing required analysis dimensions (e.g., speed metrics, sequence analysis) because they were not explicitly addressed in the code.

title: Formally define required derived metrics before segmentation
when_to_use: When the analysis requires computing complex performance or speed metrics across segmented groups.
experience:
- Identify all derived metrics required for the analysis (e.g., open_rate, click_rate, active_retention_rate_week, speed-to-activity).
- Write the exact SQL or code formula for each metric using the correct entity-level aggregation.
- Compute these metrics for the entire population to establish a baseline before segmentation.
- Then segment the data by the required dimensions (e.g., time windows, subject themes) and recompute metrics per segment.
- Compare segment metrics against the overall baseline to compute deltas and relative performance.
common_failure_prevented: Reporting segment-level metrics without baseline comparison, or missing required derived metrics entirely.

title: Design and implement sequence analysis for event data
when_to_use: When the task requires analyzing user journey sequences or event transitions.
experience:
- Identify event tables and key sequence columns (e.g., person_id, occurred_at, event_type).
- Create a chronological event sequence per user (or user-session) using window functions.
- Compute transition matrices between event types (e.g., email_open → order) and calculate transition probabilities.
- Analyze sequence patterns for key segments (e.g., high-retention users) and compare against overall patterns.
- Report findings such as most common paths, conversion rates from specific touchpoints, and sequence length distributions.
common_failure_prevented: Overlooking sequence analysis requirements despite having event-level data, resulting in incomplete analysis.
